headline: Aalto University inverted a standing rule of atomic layer deposition: halving how much film each cycle leaves drove zinc oxide 45 percent deeper into a 2,000-to-1 channel at the same dose, because depth scales as the inverse square root of per-cycle uptake.

items.title: Slower growth per cycle coats a deeper hole, and coats it sooner
items.dek: An Aalto University group halved the per-cycle growth of a zinc-oxide atomic layer deposition process — the coating that adds at most a monolayer per cycle — by dosing methanol first, and the film then reached 45 percent deeper into a 2,000-to-1 channel on the same reactant exposure.
items.why_it_matters: Coating a deep narrow feature is limited by how far reactant diffuses before the surface consumes it, so the standard fix is a longer dose, and dose time is most of what a high-aspect-ratio recipe spends. The depth reached goes as the inverse square root of what each cycle adsorbs while the dose needed to saturate the feature goes linearly with it, so cutting uptake buys back more time than it costs in extra cycles: the authors' worked example puts the saturation dose 71 percent lower.
items.background_md: Atomic layer deposition builds a film by alternating two gas pulses, each of which reacts with the surface until it runs out of sites and stops. That self-limiting step is what makes thickness uniform — but only where the surface actually saw enough reactant. Inside a trench tens of micrometres deep and a few hundred nanometres wide, molecules arrive by Knudsen diffusion, bouncing off the walls more often than off each other, and are eaten on the way in, so the growth front stalls partway down. How deep it gets for a given dose is the figure of merit the field argues about.
items.deeper_md:
The simulations are one-dimensional diffusion–reaction with reversible Langmuir adsorption, swept over Knudsen numbers across eleven orders of magnitude, sticking coefficients of 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001, and adsorption capacities q₀ from 0.5 to 8 molecules per square nanometre. In the Knudsen limit the normalised half-coverage penetration depth goes as (x/H)θ=0.5 = C·q₀^−0.5.

The experiment ran diethylzinc and water on Chipmetrics PillarHall LHAR5b chips — a 500 nm gap 1,000 µm long, aspect ratio 2,000:1 — for 180 cycles at 150, 175 and 200 °C, with a methanol pulse ahead of the diethylzinc to block adsorption sites. At 150 °C growth per cycle fell from 0.165 to 0.072 nm and q₀ from 6.6 to 3.3 nm⁻², and penetration rose from (x/H)θ=0.5 = 297 to 430, a 44.6 percent gain; at 200 °C it was 57.7 percent. XRR film density was unchanged at 5.3 g/cm³, so conformality was not bought with a worse film.

What it costs: 180 cycles now give 12.9 nm instead of 29.7 nm, so a target thickness needs about 2.3× the cycles. The relation is also explicitly scoped to Knudsen, diffusion-limited conditions at constant exposure, temperature moves gas density and diffusivity as well as GPC, and several measured points sit above the predicted curve. Nobody has disputed it yet; the preprint is three days old.

glossary.definition: The thickness one complete ALD cycle adds, set by how many reactant molecules the surface holds when saturated; it is usually a fraction of a monolayer, not a whole one.
Transport in a channel narrow enough that molecules collide with the walls more often than with each other, so the diffusion coefficient is set by the channel width rather than by pressure.
Adsorption capacity — how many reactant molecules stick to a square nanometre in one saturated pulse. GPC is proportional to it, which is why it is the knob the paper actually turns.
Distance into a channel at which the surface is half covered, divided by the channel height; for a 500 nm gap the number reads directly as the aspect ratio the film reached.

items.fab_angle: The test vehicle is a single purchasable silicon die: a lateral channel under a pillar-propped membrane turns a conformality question into an optical measurement along a 1,000 µm gap, with no cross-section and no FIB.

items.title: A whole wafer read below 700 millikelvin, on its own thermometer
items.dek: A VTT-led team working with the two Finnish companies that build the tool ran a 150 mm wafer of Coulomb-blockade thermometers — tunnel-junction arrays whose temperature follows from fundamental constants alone — through a cryogenic wafer prober and measured on-chip electron temperatures below 700 millikelvin.
items.why_it_matters: Screening quantum devices has meant cooling a few dies at a time in a dilution refrigerator for days apiece, so process variation across a wafer has been inferred from samples rather than measured. Getting under a kelvin on a prober turns that into a production step, and because the thermometer is primary, the number it returns carries no calibration borrowed from another instrument — which is the thing that normally goes unquantified below one kelvin.
items.background_md: Below about one kelvin nearly every thermometer is secondary: it reads a resistance or a voltage and converts it with a curve inherited from another instrument, and the error inherited with it is invisible. A Coulomb blockade thermometer is primary instead. Drive current through a long series array of small metal islands joined by tunnel junctions, and the conductance develops a dip around zero bias whose width is fixed by the thermal energy and the number of junctions. Temperature falls out of the measured curve, and nothing else has to be known.
items.deeper_md:
The relation is V₁/₂ ≃ 5.439·N·k_BT/e, with N the number of junctions in series — here 61, in a 61 × 20 array. The junctions are TiW/Al–AlO_x/TiW with a mean specific resistance of 1.988 kΩ·µm², chosen because TiW stays normal below one kelvin, so no magnet is needed to kill superconductivity in the electrodes. Each device carries 10 µm of electroplated copper, which does two jobs: bulk with strong electron–phonon coupling to thermalise the electrons, and a soft surface so probe needles make repeatable low-resistance contact.

On a Bluefors/AEM Afore prober with a ³He stage, the chuck was swept 0.60–1.95 K and 12 of the wafer's 24 reticles were measured. Array tunnel resistance moved by less than ±0.1 percent per device across that whole range. The previous public mark for this class of tool was Intel's 300 mm spin-qubit prober campaign at 1.6 K.

Caveats, and they are the authors' own. Measured electron temperature stayed above the chuck setpoint, attributed to residual radiative heating, imperfect thermal contact or a calibration offset. Probe contact quality varied and noisy traces were dropped. The Simmons model did not describe the background conductance, so an empirical composite background was fitted, and that fit degrades as the dip broadens with temperature. Note also that engineers from Bluefors and AEM Afore, who sell the prober, are co-authors.

glossary.definition: Suppression of tunnelling current near zero bias when the energy cost of putting one more electron on a small island exceeds the thermal energy available; how much it is suppressed is what encodes temperature.
A measurement whose result follows from fundamental constants and known device geometry, so it needs no comparison against a previously calibrated thermometer.
Full width at half minimum of the zero-bias conductance dip; for N junctions in series it equals about 5.439·N·k_BT/e, which is the whole thermometer in one line.
A thousandth of a kelvin. Superconducting and spin qubits run in the tens of millikelvin, so a prober at 700 mK is a screening instrument, not an operating environment.

items.fab_angle: Wafer-level test at temperature is the unglamorous half of any quantum-device programme, and the limiting detail here is mechanical rather than cryogenic: the 10 µm copper plating exists partly so that a needle lands softly enough to give the same contact resistance twice.

items.title: Find a crack by the detour it forces the current to take
items.dek: A group at Institute of Science Tokyo and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries pushed one amp per square millimetre through copper and imaged the magnetic field above it with nitrogen-vacancy defects in diamond, locating a 38-micrometre surface crack from the way current bends around it.
items.why_it_matters: Seen from far enough away the detour looks like a single current dipole, which is five fitted numbers rather than an image, so locating a flaw becomes a least-squares problem that works on copper — a material magnetic flux leakage cannot inspect at all. Sizing the flaw is a different result: the fitted depth missed the known geometry by up to three orders of magnitude, and the effective volume by up to four.
items.background_md: Non-destructive inspection has to infer a geometry inside a conductor from something measurable outside it, and that inverse problem has no unique solution — every method buys tractability by assuming a shape. Eddy-current probes drive an alternating field into the part and read the reaction, but resolution is set by coil size and by lift-off, the standoff between probe and surface, which changes the signal as much as a defect does. Magnetic flux leakage needs a ferromagnet. Ultrasound has a dead zone near the surface set by pulse bandwidth.
items.deeper_md:
A defect blocks conduction; current detours around its perimeter; the difference between the perturbed and unperturbed current density integrates to an effective dipole pointing against the background flow, whose far field falls as 1/r³. That is what makes position fittable rather than merely visible.

The readout is a wide-field quantum diamond microscope: 532 nm excitation over a roughly 500 µm spot, optically detected magnetic resonance read on a CCD across a 420 × 420 µm field with 8 × 8 pixel binning, the diamond sitting in contact with the specimen. At a nominal 1 A/mm² they resolved a scribed front-surface defect 38 µm long, about 5 µm wide and 1 µm deep, and an 820 × 120 × 200 µm defect on the far side of a 0.5 mm copper plate. The size metric is V_eff = |Q|/|J₀| — dipole moment over current density — which sidesteps reconstructing the shape.

The error budget is the honest part. Depth and effective volume are off by three and four orders of magnitude respectively, which the authors attribute to an uncharacterised sensor-to-specimen gap and to local current density differing from the assumed bulk value. On ferromagnetic steel the fitted dipoles point along the current instead of against it, so permeability contrast breaks the model rather than degrading it.

glossary.definition: A compact stand-in for a localized disturbance in a current distribution — equal and opposite current sources a short distance apart — whose magnetic field falls off as the inverse cube of distance.
A nitrogen atom sitting next to a vacancy in diamond; its electron-spin resonance frequency shifts with magnetic field, which turns each camera pixel above it into a magnetometer.

Optically detected magnetic resonance: sweep a microwave frequency while watching the diamond fluoresce, and the frequency of the dip gives the field through the gyromagnetic ratio of 28 GHz per tesla.
The standoff between an inspection probe and the surface under it. In eddy-current testing a change in lift-off mimics a defect, which is why it is the dominant noise source there.

items.fab_angle: The same instrument class has already been pointed at packaged integrated circuits, resolving all three field components at about 10 µm over a 3.7 × 3.7 mm window — failure analysis with no decapsulation and no needle on a pad.

items.title: A Hopper tensor core rounds every matrix multiply up to 64 rows
items.dek: KTH researchers profiled the vLLM serving stack on an NVIDIA H100 NVL and found that during token-by-token decoding a batch of one fills 1.56 percent of each 64-row fragment the Hopper tensor-core instruction insists on, while the utilisation counter reports that work as done.
items.why_it_matters: Anyone sizing a cluster reads streaming-multiprocessor utilisation as though it measured work, and in decode it does not: the counter charges a padded 64-row multiply at full price. The gap is not recoverable headroom, because the hardware has no narrower instruction to issue — so it is an argument for changing the batch size, the kernel or the metric, and not for waiting on a driver.
items.background_md: A transformer is served in two modes that stress a chip differently. Prefill consumes a whole prompt at once, so its matrix multiplies are tall and the machine is genuinely busy. Decode emits one token per request per step, which turns the same weight matrices into multiplications against as many rows as there are concurrent requests — often a handful. Tensor cores are built for the first case: they take operands in fixed-size tiles and pad whatever does not fill one. Utilisation counters were designed around issue rate and occupancy, and a padded lane is indistinguishable from a busy one.
items.deeper_md:
Hopper's warpgroup instruction has a fixed m64 × n{8–256} × k16 shape in bfloat16, so fragment fill is η_m = M/(⌈M/64⌉·64): 1.56 percent at batch 1, 3.12 at 2, 6.25 at 4, 12.5 at 8, and 5.86 percent averaged over the decode sweep. Cold prefill fills 100 percent, warm prefill 70.2.

A second rounding sits on top. The H100 NVL has 132 SMs and work is issued in waves of at most 132 thread blocks, so a kernel launching 80 leaves 52 SMs idle for that wave's full duration. Measured: 132 blocks for Qwen3-14B (no waste), 96 for Llama-3-8B (27.3 percent), 80 for Qwen3-32B (39.4 percent).

Put together, decode reports 9.4 percent SM-busy while touching 96–132 SMs and looking compute-bound, yet 70–84 percent of warp cycles are memory-dependency stalls, and useful arithmetic against the 835 TFLOP/s bfloat16 peak works out near 0.11 percent — an 8–64× overstatement. The paper is careful about what that is: "a metric-interpretation claim, not a recoverable-headroom claim." It is also scoped to one H100 SKU, one GPU with no tensor parallelism, bfloat16 rather than FP8, and a synthetic prefix-cache hit rate above 99 percent the authors call unrealistic for production traffic.

glossary.definition: Hopper's asynchronous warpgroup matrix-multiply instruction. One issue consumes a fixed tile 64 rows tall, so a smaller operand is padded out rather than the instruction being made narrower.
The phase of language-model serving that emits one token per request per step, which makes every weight matrix multiply against only as many rows as there are requests batched together.
One of the 132 independent compute blocks on an H100. "SM-busy" counts the fraction of elapsed time an SM had work issued to it, not how much of that work was real.
The rounding loss when a kernel's thread-block count is not a multiple of the SM count, so the final wave leaves part of the chip idle for its whole duration.

items.title: When a weight is a codebook index, multiply the activations first
items.dek: A Duke University group's accelerator design, Vortex, stores language-model weights as two 8-bit codebook indices per group of eight numbers and switches between two ways of executing that on a systolic array, with the crossover at a batch of 16 rows.
items.why_it_matters: Compressing weights to two bits cuts memory traffic and then gives the saving back at the multiplier, because every cell of a systolic array wanting its own codebook read at its own moment is the worst access pattern that structure has — a quantised Llama2-7B has been measured running 1.88× slower than the full-precision model on a GPU for exactly that reason. Choosing per layer whether to rebuild the weights or pre-multiply the activations is what converts the compression back into speed.
items.background_md: Vector quantisation replaces a group of weights with an index into a shared codebook, so eight numbers cost one short index instead of eight values, and the weights stop dominating memory bandwidth. The arithmetic saving does not follow automatically: somewhere the index still has to become a number. A systolic array is a grid of multiply-accumulate cells that hands operands to its neighbours on a fixed clocked schedule, which is why it is efficient and why it tolerates irregular memory access so badly. Dequantisation logic can end up costing more than the multiply it feeds.
items.deeper_md:
Two dataflows, one crossover. Lookup-first decodes indices into full weight tiles and runs an ordinary matrix multiply on a 32 × 32 FP16 array. Multiply-first never reconstructs the weights at all: it multiplies each activation row against the 512-entry codebook once, builds a partial-sum table, then uses the weight indices to index that table and accumulate. Building the table costs one pass per activation row, so it amortises badly at batch 1 and well at batch 64; the analytical model puts the two arrangements equal at M = 16, which is why the design keeps both and switches on batch size.

Configuration is n = 2 codebooks, vector length v = 8, b = 8 bits per index — 2 bits per weight and an 8.0 kB FP16 codebook small enough to stay on chip. Synthesised at 28 nm and 500 MHz the design is 2.10 mm² with 336 kB of SRAM and 10.6 W peak, of which DDR4 is 67 percent.

Read the speedups through their decomposition rather than the headline. The quantised kernel alone is 31.1×; that becomes 11.33× on fully connected layers and 22.4× end to end against an 8-bit systolic baseline, because attention is not quantised. Contextual sparsity contributes 1.19× and fades as batch grows. All of it is simulation, not measured silicon.

glossary.definition: Replacing a group of weights with one index into a shared codebook of representative vectors, so the stored cost per weight is the index width divided by the group size — here 8 bits over 8 weights, twice.
A grid of multiply-accumulate cells that passes operands to its neighbours on a fixed clocked schedule; high throughput, and almost no tolerance for a cell needing its own unpredictable memory read.
Eight-bit weights with eight-bit activations, the conventional quantised configuration used here as the baseline both speedup and energy figures are measured against.
The number of activation rows entering a matrix multiply, which equals how many sequences are being served at once, and decides whether the operation is a tall matrix product or nearly a vector one.

items.title: One writeback thread per device is a ceiling nobody measures
items.dek: Mitsumasa Kondo attached in-kernel tracing probes to a PostgreSQL transaction benchmark running on Amazon block storage and found that splitting the same provisioned 80,000 IOPS across four volumes instead of one cut the number of times Linux paused a write system call by 70 percent.
items.why_it_matters: Linux runs one writeback thread per block device, so the rate at which dirty pages leave memory is capped per device rather than per unit of provisioned bandwidth. On network-attached storage, where a single write costs far more latency than on a local SSD, that one drain falls behind and the kernel starts sleeping the application's write calls — and none of those pauses show up in iostat or /proc/diskstats, so the stall gets attributed to the database instead.
items.background_md: A buffered write does not reach storage. It marks a page dirty in memory and returns, and a kernel thread writes it out later, which is why write() is fast and why the kernel needs some way to stop a process dirtying pages faster than they can be drained. Since 2011 Linux does that by computing a sleep interval and pausing the offending process, rather than making it perform the writeback itself, which produced terrible I/O patterns. The assumption underneath the design is a local disk with a deep queue and tens of microseconds of latency.
items.deeper_md:
Setup: an AWS c6in.8xlarge running Rocky Linux 9.8 on kernel 5.14, PostgreSQL 16.4, TPC-C at 1,000 warehouses (about 100 GB) with 256 virtual users, on gp3 volumes provisioned to the same 80K IOPS and 2.0 GB/s in every configuration. eBPF programs on the `writeback:writeback_start` and `writeback:written` tracepoints separate flusher-thread I/O from foreground I/O, and `writeback:balance_dirty_pages` counts each throttle pause.

One volume: 2,513 throttle episodes, 679.4 MB/s of write bandwidth, 444,326 new-order transactions per minute, 1,238 ms worst-case latency. Four volumes at identical total provisioning: 755 episodes, 827.1 MB/s, 544,354 NOPM, 502 ms — 70.0 percent fewer pauses, 23 percent more throughput, 59.4 percent lower tail latency. Holding IOPS and bandwidth constant is what makes the number of drains the only variable; the paper also notes the cloud block device exposes only two I/O queues for QoS isolation, which is the second half of the congestion.

Caveats: this is a conference poster, one workload on one cloud, and the author is the same person who published the multi-volume layout used as the experimental lever, so the comparison is between his own configurations. He states that the interaction with the kernel's dirty-ratio tunables is not yet characterised.

glossary.definition: A page of memory holding data an application has written but the kernel has not yet sent to storage; the kernel owes that write and chooses when to issue it.
Linux's method, merged in 2011, of slowing a process that dirties pages too fast by sleeping it for a computed interval capped at 200 ms, instead of making it do the writeback itself.
Provisioned I/O operations per second, the unit cloud block storage is sold in. It bounds the request rate and says nothing about how many kernel threads will be available to issue those requests.
New orders per minute, the TPC-C throughput metric, counting completed new-order transactions rather than raw I/O operations.

items.title: Train the attention selector on the loss it is actually hurting
items.dek: A Tencent and HKUST team trained the block selector inside a sparse-attention model directly against the language-modelling loss by adding its score in log form to the attention logits, and at a 1,024-token budget Qwen3-4B scored 90.65 on MATH500 against 84.67 for the distillation-trained baseline.
items.why_it_matters: Every trainable sparse-attention scheme has to make a discrete choice — which blocks of context to read — differentiable somehow, and the usual answer is to train the selector to imitate the attention map of the full model. That gives the selector a target that is only a proxy for the quantity anyone cares about, and the proxy fails hardest where the budget is tightest and a wrong pick cannot be recovered from later in the sequence.
items.background_md: Attention costs time and memory in proportion to how much context each query reads, so long-context serving stacks all try to read less of it: score the context in blocks, keep the top few, skip the rest. The obstacle is that top-k selection is a step function of the scores and passes no gradient, so whatever produced those scores cannot be trained by the same backward pass that trains the rest of the network. The standing workarounds are a cheap proxy score computed at inference time, or a separately trained scorer.
items.deeper_md:
The mechanism is where the gate sits. In training, SAS normalises the selector's block scores and adds their logarithm to the attention logits before the softmax — softmax(qKᵀ + log g_S)V_S — with the current block pinned at unit gain. Multiplying after the softmax would be the obvious move and is the wrong one: adding in log space leaves the selector inside the normalisation, so gradient from the language-modelling loss reaches it. Scores stay continuous through training and are discretised into a hard top-k only at inference.

Setup: Qwen3 at 4B, 8B and 14B plus OLMo3-7B, one epoch of OpenR1-Math-220K at 32,768 tokens, block size 64, budgets of 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 tokens, against SeerAttention-R using an identical selector trained by self-distillation. Gains concentrate at the tight end — GPQA-Diamond 50.41 versus 39.84 at a 1,024-token budget on the 4B model — and shrink toward dense as the budget grows. Worth keeping in view: full attention is 93.93 and 56.19 on those two, so the sparse gap narrows rather than closing.

The authors report slower early convergence under sparse-scope training, and the training corpus is mathematics, so the long-context and agentic results are transfer rather than in-domain.

glossary.definition: The number of context tokens a query is permitted to read at each step. Fixing it makes decode cost constant in context length rather than growing with it.
Keeping only the k highest-scoring context blocks. It is a step function of the scores, so it passes no gradient back to whatever computed them — which is the whole difficulty.
The pre-softmax score for one key. Adding a quantity here multiplies the resulting attention weight, which is why a gain is applied in log form rather than directly.
Training a small selector to reproduce the attention pattern of the full model it sits inside, using that model's own attention as the target instead of the task loss.

foundations.topic: The von Neumann architecture and its bottleneck
foundations.subtitle: One memory for both the program and the numbers — the decision that made software a thing, and the traffic jam it built in on page one.
foundations.tldr: In 1945 a report on a machine that was never built as described laid out five organs — arithmetic, control, memory, input, output — and put the instructions in the same memory as the numbers. That single choice is why software exists as something separable from hardware, and why a computer can be changed by writing rather than by rewiring. It also means every instruction and every operand travels the same path to the same store, and eighty-one years later that path, not the arithmetic, is what most programs spend their time waiting on.

sections.heading: Before 1945, changing the program meant changing the machine
sections.body_md:
Start from the constraint the 1945 report was written against. ENIAC computed by having its function units physically wired together for one problem; switching problems meant re-plugging cables and resetting switches, work measured in days. The machine was fast and the setup was not, so the setup dominated.

The move in the *First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC* is stated almost in passing, in §2.4(b): "The instructions which govern a complicated problem may constitute a considerable material, particularly so, if the code is circumstantial (which it is in most arrangements). This material must be remembered." Orders are not a wiring diagram. They are material, like intermediate results and function tables, and material goes in the memory.

Once the orders live in the same store as the numbers, changing the program is a write. That is the whole idea, and everything a modern system does — compilers, loaders, operating systems, a JIT rewriting itself while it runs — follows from it.

sections.heading: Five organs, and the compromise inside them
sections.body_md:
The report's §2 names five specific parts. §2.2 gives CA, the central arithmetic organ, on the grounds that "since the device is primarily a computer, it will have to perform the elementary operations of arithmetics most frequently." §2.3 gives CC, central control: "the logical control of the device, that is the proper sequencing of its operations can be most efficiently carried out by a central control organ." §2.5 gives M: "the total memory constitutes the third specific part of the device." §2.7 and §2.8 give I and O, the organs that move information in from and out to the outside recording medium.

That list is the block diagram on the first page of every architecture textbook since. What the textbooks usually drop is the reason the parts are arranged the way they are. §5.6: the device should be as simple as possible, that is, contain as few elements as possible — achieved by "never performing two operations simultaneously, if this would cause a significant increase" in the elements needed.

sections.heading: Trading time for parts was the right call, and then it wasn't
sections.body_md:
In 1945 the scarce resource was vacuum tubes. They were expensive, they drew power, and they failed, so a design that did one thing at a time with few tubes beat one that did several things at once with many. Serialising the machine was economically correct.

Put a number on what that bought. §12 proposes a memory of about 8,000 minor cycles of 32 binary digits each — roughly 32 kilobytes — and that one store had to hold the intermediate results, the function tables, the boundary conditions *and* the program. Everything the machine knew went through one channel to one place.

The scarcity then reversed. Transistors became nearly free and the count per chip grew for fifty years, while the wire between the processor and the store did not get correspondingly wider or shorter. The architecture that was chosen because elements were expensive is now run in a world where elements are cheap and movement is expensive — which is precisely the assumption it was optimised against.

sections.heading: Backus names it, in 1978
sections.body_md:
John Backus, who had led the FORTRAN team, used his Turing Award lecture — published in *Communications of the ACM* in August 1978 as "Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?" — to give the problem its name. The von Neumann bottleneck is the connecting path between the store and the processing unit, down which the machine pumps words one at a time, and which every computation must therefore be expressed as traffic through.

His sharper claim was that the damage is not only to throughput. Because programming languages are, in his reading, high-level copies of the machine underneath them, the word-at-a-time shape propagates upward into how people are able to think about programs at all — the argument later restated as a "von Neumann vicious circle," in which non-von-Neumann hardware cannot arrive because there are no languages for it, and those languages cannot arrive because there is no hardware to found them on.

You do not have to accept the second half to find the first half measurable.

sections.heading: The bottleneck, in units
sections.body_md:
The modern form of the argument is arithmetic intensity: operations performed per byte moved. A machine has a ratio it needs in order to stay busy, and a program has a ratio it supplies; whichever is smaller decides the runtime.

The two ratios have been diverging for two decades. Over the past twenty years peak server arithmetic has grown at about 3.0× every two years — roughly 60,000× in total — while DRAM bandwidth grew at 1.6× every two years (about 100×) and interconnect bandwidth at 1.4× (about 30×). Divide the first by the second: the intensity a machine demands has risen by about 1.9× every two years. Model size, meanwhile, has grown at 410× every two years against memory capacity per accelerator at 2×.

This is why two models with comparable operation counts can differ by orders of magnitude in latency. Generating tokens one at a time turns matrix–matrix products into matrix–vector ones, the arithmetic per byte collapses, and the machine stops being a computer and becomes a memory system with an expensive accessory attached.

sections.heading: Every fix is the same fix, and the one that isn't
sections.body_md:
Look at the mitigations and they rhyme. Caches keep recently-moved bytes near the arithmetic so the next trip is shorter. Separate instruction and data caches make the top of the hierarchy Harvard while everything below it stays von Neumann. Prefetching starts the trip early; out-of-order execution finds work to do during it; wide vector and tensor instructions get more arithmetic out of each byte that arrives. None of these widens the path — they raise the operations-per-byte the program supplies, or they hide the latency.

The designs that attack the path itself — dataflow machines, processing-in-memory, analog crossbars that compute inside the array — keep almost arriving and then not. And the reason the old architecture holds is that its defining property is load-bearing elsewhere: code and data in one store is what makes a compiler possible. It is also what makes a buffer overflow executable, which is why modern hardware spends transistors on no-execute bits to partially undo, for safety, the very thing that made the machine general.

glossary.definition: A machine that holds its instructions in the same read/write memory as its data, so a program can be loaded, generated, or modified by another program rather than wired in.
The EDVAC report's unit of memory — one word's worth of circulating delay-line storage, specified at 32 binary digits, with about 8,000 of them proposed for the whole machine.
Operations performed per byte moved from memory, in FLOP/byte. Compare a program's value to the machine's ratio of peak arithmetic to peak bandwidth: the smaller of the two sets the achievable rate.

Separate storage and separate paths for instructions and for data. Modern processors are Harvard at the first-level caches and von Neumann below them, which is why self-modifying code needs an explicit instruction-cache flush.
The standing name for the widening gap between how fast a processor can compute and how fast memory can feed it, which grows because the two improve at different exponential rates.

A per-page hardware permission saying memory may be read but not executed as instructions — an after-the-fact partial retraction of the stored-program idea, added because code and data sharing one store is also how code injection works.

foundations.try_this: Open the Internet Archive's full text of the First Draft and read §§2.2 through 2.8 — five short paragraphs that name the five organs — then §5.6, where the report justifies doing one operation at a time on the grounds that vacuum tubes were the scarce part. Then make the bottleneck a number you own: take one inner loop from anything you have written, count the bytes it must fetch per iteration and the arithmetic operations it performs on them, and divide. Compare that ratio against what the hardware demands, remembering that the demanded ratio has been climbing at roughly 3.0 ÷ 1.6, or about 1.9×, every two years. If your loop supplies less than the machine demands, no amount of faster arithmetic will help it, and you have just reproduced the 1945 design decision as a measurement on your own code.
